title: Sparse Embeddings
description: Discover how words and documents are turned into vectors before neural embeddings existed.
content:
To feed text to a model we must turn tokens into numbers. **Sparse representations** give every term a dimension in a vocabulary-sized vector space.

> Sparse representations, from simplest to strongest:
> • **One-hot** - each word is a vector with a single 1 at its own index; all words are mutually orthogonal, so similarity cannot be expressed, and vectors are huge and mostly zeros
> • **Bag-of-words (BOW)** - a document is a vector of term counts; word order is ignored ('dog bites man' becomes the same vector as 'man bites dog')
> • **TF-IDF** - weights counts by informativeness: tf-idf(t, d) = tf(t, d) × log(N / (1 + df(t))), where tf is the term frequency in the document, df the document frequency, and N the corpus size
> • **BM25** - a probabilistic ranking function that combines IDF with **term-frequency saturation** (controlled by k1) and **document-length normalization** (controlled by b); the standard baseline for search ranking

The intuition behind TF-IDF: words frequent in a document but rare across the corpus (like 'kernel') are informative, while words frequent everywhere (like 'the') get low weight. BM25 refines this idea: the benefit of the 10th occurrence of a term is smaller than that of the 1st (saturation), and long documents are dampened so they do not dominate purely by length. Documents compared in these spaces are the basis of classic **information retrieval**.
